lessons.title: Building and reading generating functions
lessons.summary: Encode a discrete distribution in the coefficients and powers of one function.
lessons.objective: Construct a valid PGF and recover probabilities, support and named count models.
lessons.before: Review discrete probability, binomial and Poisson models, and geometric series. Unlike a continuous density, a discrete mass function assigns probabilities to individual values.
lessons.ideas:
A distribution written as a power series

For a non-negative integer-valued X, attach probability P(X=r) to the power tʳ. The variable t is an algebraic input; it is not the outcome.

\[\begin{gathered}G_X(t)=\mathrm E(t^X)=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}p_rt^r\\p_r\ge0,\qquad \sum_{r=0}^{\infty}p_r=1\\G_X(1)=1,\qquad G_X(0)=\mathrm P(X=0)\end{gathered}\]

Every missing power has coefficient zero. Normalisation alone is insufficient: a negative coefficient cannot represent a probability. For finite support the series is a polynomial. An infinite probability series converges at least for |t|≤1; a closed rational expression must be interpreted with its series and convergence range.

Recognise common constructions

\[\begin{gathered}X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p):\quad G_X(t)=(1-p+pt)^n\\X\sim\operatorname{Po}(\lambda):\quad G_X(t)=e^{\lambda(t-1)}\\T=\text{trials including first success}:\quad G_T(t)=\frac{pt}{1-(1-p)t}\\F=\text{failures before success}:\quad G_F(t)=\frac{p}{1-(1-p)t}\end{gathered}\]

The geometric model needs independent trials with a constant success probability, 0<p<1. Its two counting conventions differ by one. For a capped process, the final value includes every path that reaches the cap, even paths with no success.

Coefficient extraction and integer tails

\[\begin{gathered}\mathrm P(X=r)=[t^r]G_X(t)=\frac{G_X^{(r)}(0)}{r!}\end{gathered}\]

Use derivatives at 0 for coefficients, not at 1. For geometric tails, translate a strict event such as X<N into the actual integer values before using a complement. After a logarithmic inequality, check both neighbouring integers. Division by a negative logarithm reverses the inequality.
lessons.method:
1. State the support and the mass at each value.
  2. Form the defining expectation or power series.
  3. Sum or factorise the expression, with its appropriate domain.
  4. Check non-negative coefficients and G(1)=1.
  5. Read the requested coefficient or sum the correct integer tail.
mistakes: Exponents are values of the count, not probabilities.
G(1)=1 does not excuse a negative coefficient.
Trials including success and failures before success have different supports.
Keep strict and inclusive integer tails distinct.
The coefficient formula uses derivatives at 0 and divides by r factorial.

examples.title: 1 · Read the powers as possible counts
examples.question: A batch count \(X\) takes values \(0,2,4\) with probabilities \(\frac25,\frac15,\frac25\). Build its PGF and find \(\mathrm P(X=3)\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_X(t)=\frac25+\frac15t^2+\frac25t^4\\G_X(1)=1,\qquad [t^3]G_X(t)=0\end{gathered}\]

Each probability multiplies a power whose exponent is the count. There is no degree-3 term, so that value is impossible. A missing term means zero probability.

examples.title: 2 · Count attempts or count failures
examples.question: Independent trials succeed with probability \(\frac27\). Let \(T\) include the first success, and let \(F\) count only the preceding failures. Derive both PGFs and find \(\mathrm P(T>4)\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mathrm P(T=r)=\frac27\left(\frac57\right)^{r-1},\quad r\ge1\\G_T(t)=\frac{2t}{7}\sum_{j=0}^\infty\left(\frac{5t}{7}\right)^j=\frac{2t}{7-5t}\\G_F(t)=\frac{2}{7-5t}\\\mathrm P(T>4)=\left(\frac57\right)^4=\frac{625}{2401}\end{gathered}\]

The two supports start at 1 and 0 respectively. Both series converge for \(|t|<\frac75\). More than four attempts requires the first four trials to fail.

examples.title: 3 · A finite uniform count
examples.question: A random setting \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1,2,3\}\). Find its PGF as a polynomial and as a fraction, and explain the value at \(t=1\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_X(t)=\frac{1+t+t^2+t^3}{4}\\G_X(t)=\frac{1-t^4}{4(1-t)},\quad t\ne1\\G_X(1)=1\end{gathered}\]

The fraction is a finite geometric-sum identity. Its apparent singularity at 1 is removable: the original polynomial is defined there, and its coefficients sum to 1.

examples.title: 4 · A Poisson count and its parity
examples.question: \(X\) is Poisson with mean \(\frac43\). Derive its PGF from the mass function and find the probability that \(X\) is even, including zero.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_X(t)=e^{-4/3}\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{(4t/3)^r}{r!}=e^{\frac43(t-1)}\\G_X(-1)=\mathrm P(\text{even})-\mathrm P(\text{odd})=e^{-8/3}\\\mathrm P(\text{even})=\frac{1+e^{-8/3}}2\end{gathered}\]

The two parity probabilities also sum to 1. Evaluating at −1 changes the signs of the odd-power terms; it does not discard them.

lessons.title: Recovering distributions and moments
lessons.summary: Use derivatives at one, and keep ordinary and factorial moments separate.
lessons.objective: Find means and variances from PGFs and recover unknown probability parameters.
lessons.before: Complete building and reading PGFs. Review differentiation, linear equations and Var(X)=E(X²)−[E(X)]².
lessons.ideas:
Why the evaluation point changes

Differentiating each term multiplies its coefficient by the exponent. Evaluation at 1 then sums the weighted probabilities. Where these moments are finite,

\[\begin{gathered}G'_X(1)=\sum_r rp_r=\mathrm E(X)\\G''_X(1)=\sum_r r(r-1)p_r=\mathrm E[X(X-1)]\\\mathrm E(X^2)=G''_X(1)+G'_X(1)\\\operatorname{Var}(X)=G''_X(1)+G'_X(1)-[G'_X(1)]^2\end{gathered}\]

For an infinite distribution, use the derivative at 1 or its left limit when the defining series requires it. An infinite moment is not made finite by formal substitution. All models used in the written questions here have the moments required.

Recover coefficients by independent conditions

Start with normalisation. A known mean gives a first weighted equation; a known variance gives a second-moment equation after adding the square of the mean. Solve all equations together and check non-negativity. A negative algebraic solution is not a valid probability.

Parameters have restrictions

A binomial trial count is a non-negative integer and its success probability is between 0 and 1. A Poisson parameter is positive. For repeated-copy reconstruction, the candidate root must be a probability series, not merely an algebraic root. The original model restrictions decide which solutions remain.
lessons.method:
1. Normalise any unknown coefficients.
  2. Differentiate before substituting t=1.
  3. Record the first and second factorial moments.
  4. Convert to E(X²) and variance.
  5. Solve remaining parameters and check all probability and model restrictions.
mistakes: G″(1) is not E(X²).
Subtract the square of the mean, not the mean itself.
Use derivatives at 1 for moments, at 0 for coefficients.
Check every recovered coefficient is non-negative.
A formal root or non-integral binomial trial count may be inadmissible.

examples.title: 1 · The second derivative is a factorial moment
examples.question: For \(G_X(t)=\frac{3+2t+t^3}{6}\), find \(\mathrm E(X)\), \(\mathrm E(X^2)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G'_X(1)=\frac56,\qquad G''_X(1)=1\\\mathrm E(X^2)=1+\frac56=\frac{11}{6}\\\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{11}{6}-\left(\frac56\right)^2=\frac{41}{36}\end{gathered}\]

The second derivative supplies E[X(X−1)]. Add the first moment before subtracting the square of the mean.

examples.title: 2 · Reconstruct all probabilities
examples.question: \(X\) takes values \(0,1,2\). Its mean is \(\frac76\) and variance is \(\frac{17}{36}\). Recover its whole PGF.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}a+b+c=1\\b+2c=\frac76\\b+4c=\frac{17}{36}+\left(\frac76\right)^2=\frac{11}{6}\\c=\frac13,\quad b=\frac12,\quad a=\frac16\\G_X(t)=\frac{1+3t+2t^2}{6}\end{gathered}\]

Subtract the two moment equations to find c, then solve for the other coefficients. All three are non-negative and sum to 1; these checks are part of reconstructing a distribution.

examples.title: 3 · A shifted infinite-support model
examples.question: A count has \(G_X(t)=\frac{t^2}{5-4t}\). Use its PGF to find the mean and variance.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_X(t)=t^2\frac{1/5}{1-(4/5)t}\\G'_X(1)=6,\qquad G''_X(1)=50\\\operatorname{Var}(X)=50+6-6^2=20\end{gathered}\]

The factor t² shifts a geometric failure count by 2. The mean shifts, while the variance is unchanged by that constant. Direct differentiation agrees with this interpretation.

examples.title: 4 · Recover a binomial model from two moments
examples.question: \(X\) is binomial with unknown \(n,p\). Its mean is \(3\) and variance is \(\frac94\). Recover \(n,p\) and the PGF.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_X(t)=(1-p+pt)^n\\G'_X(1)=np,\qquad G''_X(1)=n(n-1)p^2\\np=3,\qquad np(1-p)=\frac94\\p=\frac14,\qquad n=12\\G_X(t)=\left(\frac34+\frac14t\right)^{12}\end{gathered}\]

The ratio of variance to mean is 1−p. The resulting n must be a positive integer and p must lie in [0,1].

lessons.title: Adding independent counts
lessons.summary: Use products only when the component counts are independent.
lessons.objective: Construct the PGF of an independent sum and extract its probabilities and moments.
lessons.before: Complete moments. Review products of polynomials and independence of random variables.
lessons.ideas:
From the joint expectation to a product

\[\begin{gathered}G_{X+Y}(t)=\mathrm E(t^{X+Y})=\mathrm E(t^Xt^Y)\\=\mathrm E(t^X)\mathrm E(t^Y)=G_X(t)G_Y(t)\quad\text{if X,Y are independent}\\\mathrm P(X+Y=r)=\sum_j\mathrm P(X=j)\mathrm P(Y=r-j)\end{gathered}\]

This coefficient sum is convolution. Include every contributing pair, weighted by its probability. Sampling without replacement can determine a hypergeometric count within one experiment; that count can still be independent of a separately randomised experiment.

Moments from the product rule

\[\begin{gathered}G'_{X+Y}(1)=G'_X(1)+G'_Y(1)\\G''_{X+Y}(1)=G''_X(1)+2G'_X(1)G'_Y(1)+G''_Y(1)\\\mathrm E(X+Y)=\mathrm E(X)+\mathrm E(Y)\\\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)\quad\text{under independence}\end{gathered}\]

The mean identity also holds without independence when the expectations exist. The PGF product and the variance identity require independence here. Keep the product factorised for differentiation when that is shorter; expand only as far as the requested coefficient needs.
lessons.method:
1. Build each component PGF with the correct within-experiment model.
  2. Justify independence of the component counts.
  3. Multiply their PGFs.
  4. Collect all contributions to the requested total.
  5. Differentiate the product or add independently justified moments.
mistakes: A product of PGFs requires independent counts.
Dependence between draws and dependence between final counts are different issues.
Add every coefficient contribution for a total.
A product of two coefficients of degree r does not give the degree-r coefficient of a product.
Equal means do not identify a distribution.

examples.title: 1 · Convolution appears as multiplication
examples.question: Independent counts have \(G_X(t)=\frac{3+2t}{5}\) and \(G_Y(t)=\frac{2+t^2}{3}\). Find the PGF of \(Z=X+Y\) and \(\mathrm P(Z=2)\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_Z(t)=G_X(t)G_Y(t)\\=\frac{6+4t+3t^2+2t^3}{15}\\\mathrm P(Z=2)=\frac15\end{gathered}\]

The degree-2 coefficient comes from X=0 and Y=2. Coefficients of other degrees collect every pair with that total. Independence allows each joint probability to factor.

examples.title: 2 · Dependence inside one selection is allowed
examples.question: Choose two counters without replacement from three marked and four unmarked counters; \(X\) counts marked counters. Independently generate a binary \(Y\) with \(\mathrm P(Y=1)=\frac25\). Find \(G_{X+Y}(t)\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mathrm P(X=r)=\frac{\binom3r\binom4{2-r}}{\binom72}\\G_X(t)=\frac{6+12t+3t^2}{21}\\G_{X+Y}(t)=\frac{18+48t+33t^2+6t^3}{105}\end{gathered}\]

The two draws within the counter selection are dependent, so X is not binomial. The completed count X is independent of Y, which is exactly the independence needed for their sum.

examples.title: 3 · Add independent Poisson counts
examples.question: Independent counts \(X,Y\) are Poisson with means \(\frac23,\frac56\). Identify \(Z=X+Y\) using its PGF.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_Z(t)=e^{\frac23(t-1)}e^{\frac56(t-1)}\\=e^{\frac32(t-1)}\\Z\sim\operatorname{Po}(3/2)\end{gathered}\]

Multiplication adds the exponents. The resulting expression is a Poisson PGF with parameter equal to the sum of the two parameters. Independence is necessary for this argument.

examples.title: 4 · Two waiting times with different probabilities
examples.question: Independent waiting times include their first successes, with success probabilities \(\frac25,\frac34\). Find \(\mathrm P(X+Y=3)\), and the mean and variance of their total.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_Z(t)=\frac{6t^2}{(5-3t)(4-t)}\\\mathrm P(Z=3)=\frac25\frac34\left(\frac35+\frac14\right)=\frac{51}{200}\\\mathrm E(Z)=\frac52+\frac43=\frac{23}{6}\\\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{15}{4}+\frac49=\frac{151}{36}\end{gathered}\]

The coefficient has two contributions: waiting-time pairs (1,2) and (2,1). These probabilities differ, so counting the pairs without weighting them would be wrong.

lessons.title: Transformations and dependence
lessons.summary: Distinguish changing one outcome from combining independent outcomes.
lessons.objective: Transform supported values correctly and recognise products, mixtures and conditional models.
lessons.before: Complete independent sums. Review conditional probability and the support of a transformed variable.
lessons.ideas:
Start from the defining expectation

\[\begin{gathered}Y=aX+b\quad\Longrightarrow\quad G_Y(t)=t^bG_X(t^a)\end{gathered}\]

For the ordinary PGF convention, ensure the transformed values remain non-negative integers. A finite distribution can also be represented by a Laurent expression when negative outcomes occur; state the convention rather than assuming an ordinary probability power series. Always inspect the mapped support.

One observation versus independent copies

\[\begin{gathered}G_{aX}(t)=G_X(t^a)\\G_{X_1+\cdots+X_a}(t)=[G_X(t)]^a\quad\text{for independent identical copies}\\\operatorname{Var}(aX)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\end{gathered}\]

The coefficient support and variances generally differ even when the means agree. Two counts derived from the same selection can be dependent; use their joint outcomes to build a total instead of multiplying marginal PGFs.

Mixtures and conditioning

\[\begin{gathered}G_X(t)=wG_{X\mid A}(t)+(1-w)G_{X\mid B}(t)\\G_{X\mid X>0}(t)=\frac{G_X(t)-p_0}{1-p_0},\quad p_0=\mathrm P(X=0)<1\end{gathered}\]

A mixture chooses exactly one mode. Conditioning keeps a specified event and renormalises its probabilities. Neither operation is an independent-sum product.
lessons.method:
1. Identify whether the experiment transforms, sums, selects a mode or conditions.
  2. Write the defining expectation or joint outcomes.
  3. Use the appropriate substitution, product or weighted sum.
  4. Check the support and normalisation.
  5. Extract the required probabilities and moments.
mistakes: G(t²) and G(t)² describe different experiments.
Shared observations do not become independent because their marginals are known.
A mixture uses a weighted sum of conditional PGFs.
Conditioning requires division by the retained probability.
Check the transformed support before calling an expression an ordinary PGF.

examples.title: 1 · Multiply the outcome, then shift it
examples.question: \(X\) has PGF \(G_X(t)=\frac{3+2t+t^2}{6}\). For \(Y=3X+2\), find the PGF and support.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_Y(t)=\mathrm E(t^{3X+2})=t^2G_X(t^3)\\=\frac{3t^2+2t^5+t^8}{6}\end{gathered}\]

The support {0,1,2} maps to {2,5,8}. Replace the input t by t³, then multiply by t². Cubing the PGF would instead describe three independent observations.

examples.title: 2 · Reusing a value is not independent repetition
examples.question: \(X\) is a binary indicator with success probability \(\frac27\). Compare \(A=2X\) with \(B=X_1+X_2\) for independent copies.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_A(t)=\frac{5+2t^2}{7}\\G_B(t)=\frac{25+20t+4t^2}{49}\\\mathrm E(A)=\mathrm E(B)=\frac47\\\operatorname{Var}(A)=\frac{40}{49}\\\operatorname{Var}(B)=\frac{20}{49}\end{gathered}\]

A cannot equal 1, but B can. Doubling one observation multiplies its variance by 4; adding two independent copies multiplies it by 2.

examples.title: 3 · Exclusive modes give a weighted sum
examples.question: A device uses mode A with probability \(\frac14\), otherwise mode B. Mode A outputs a fair binary count; mode B always outputs \(2\). Find the overall PGF, mean and variance.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_X(t)=\frac14\frac{1+t}{2}+\frac34t^2\\=\frac{1+t+6t^2}{8}\\G'_X(1)=\frac{13}{8},\qquad G''_X(1)=\frac32\\\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac32+\frac{13}{8}-\left(\frac{13}{8}\right)^2=\frac{31}{64}\end{gathered}\]

Only one mode is used. A product would describe a sum of two independently produced outputs, which is a different experiment.

examples.title: 4 · Remove zero and renormalise
examples.question: \(X\) counts successes in three independent trials with probability \(\frac25\). A recorded run has at least one success; \(Y\) is the count conditional on \(X>0\). Find its PGF and mean.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_X(t)=\left(\frac{3+2t}{5}\right)^3,\qquad p_0=\frac{27}{125}\\G_Y(t)=\frac{G_X(t)-p_0}{1-p_0}\\=\frac{27t+18t^2+4t^3}{49}\\\mathrm E(Y)=G'_Y(1)=\frac{75}{49}\end{gathered}\]

Remove just the zero coefficient, then divide every remaining coefficient by the probability of a positive run. Subtracting zero without renormalising would leave total probability below 1.

lessons.title: Repeated independent sums
lessons.summary: Power the PGF for copies, and use coefficients to handle constrained totals.
lessons.objective: Analyse repeated independent counts, reconstruct summands and calculate conditional totals.
lessons.before: Complete transformations and dependence. Review powers, coefficient extraction and conditional probability.
lessons.ideas:
More than two independent variables

\[\begin{gathered}G_{X_1+\cdots+X_n}(t)=\prod_{j=1}^nG_{X_j}(t)\\G_{S_n}(t)=[G_X(t)]^n\quad\text{for independent identical copies}\end{gathered}\]

Identical distributions do not by themselves give independence. With independent copies and finite moments, differentiating the power at 1 gives

\[\begin{gathered}G'_{S_n}(1)=nG'_X(1)\\G''_{S_n}(1)=nG''_X(1)+n(n-1)[G'_X(1)]^2\\\mathrm E(S_n)=n\mathrm E(X)\\\operatorname{Var}(S_n)=n\operatorname{Var}(X)\end{gathered}\]

Keep coefficient calculations local

When an external power of t shifts the support, remove that shift before choosing a binomial term. Several ordered combinations can give the same total. A conditional event requires its joint coefficient divided by the total-event coefficient.

Recovering the summand

If a total is known to be a sum of independent identical variables, its PGF is a power of the unknown summand PGF. Use coefficient constraints and non-negativity, or a recognised factorisation, to find the admissible root. Check the result by raising it back to the required power.
lessons.method:
1. Check independence and whether all copies have the same distribution.
  2. Form the product or power.
  3. Track the minimum total and any support gaps.
  4. Extract coefficients or differentiate before evaluating.
  5. For a conditional question divide the joint-event coefficient by the conditioning-event coefficient.
mistakes: Identical distribution is not independence.
Do not replace a power of G(t) by G(tⁿ).
Adjust the requested degree for an external power of t.
Keep every ordered contribution to a coefficient.
A reconstructed root must have non-negative coefficients and normalise to one.

examples.title: 1 · Three independent counts
examples.question: \(X\) has PGF \(G_X(t)=\frac{1+2t+t^2}{4}\). Let \(S\) be the sum of three independent copies. Find its PGF, \(\mathrm P(S=3)\), mean and variance.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_S(t)=\frac{(1+t)^6}{64}\\\mathrm P(S=3)=\frac{\binom63}{64}=\frac5{16}\\\mathrm E(S)=3,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(S)=\frac32\end{gathered}\]

The PGF identifies a binomial count with six fair trials. Differentiating the powered PGF gives the same moments as adding the three independent means and variances.

examples.title: 2 · Repetition preserves gaps in possible totals
examples.question: \(X\) takes values \(1,3\) with probabilities \(\frac45,\frac15\). Two independent copies are added. Find their total’s PGF, support and probability of \(4\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}G_S(t)=\left(\frac{4t+t^3}{5}\right)^2\\=\frac{16t^2+8t^4+t^6}{25}\\\mathrm P(S=4)=\frac8{25}\end{gathered}\]

The support is {2,4,6}. Total 4 comes from the two ordered outcomes (1,3) and (3,1). Odd totals remain impossible.

examples.title: 3 · Recover one summand
examples.question: A total of three independent identical non-negative integer-valued counts has PGF \(\frac{t^3}{(4-3t)^3}\). Recover the summand PGF and its mean.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}[G_X(t)]^3=\frac{t^3}{(4-3t)^3}\\G_X(t)=\frac{t}{4-3t}\\G'_X(t)=\frac{4}{(4-3t)^2},\qquad \mathrm E(X)=4\end{gathered}\]

The recovered function is a valid positive-integer waiting-time PGF. The probability-series conditions and value 1 at t=1 select the admissible branch; an arbitrary algebraic root is insufficient.

examples.title: 4 · Condition on a total
examples.question: Four independent fair binary observations have total \(S\). Given \(S=2\), find the probability that the first observation is zero.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mathrm P(S=2)=[t^2]\left(\frac{1+t}{2}\right)^4=\frac6{16}\\\mathrm P(X_1=0,S=2)=\frac12[t^2]\left(\frac{1+t}{2}\right)^3=\frac3{16}\\\mathrm P(X_1=0\mid S=2)=\frac{3/16}{6/16}=\frac12\end{gathered}\]

Use the unconditional independent model to compute the joint event, then divide by the probability of the conditioning total. The observations are no longer independent after conditioning on that total.

questions.title: First successful calibration
questions.prompt_html:
A calibration attempt succeeds with probability \(\frac{3}{10}\). Attempts are independent. The random variable \(X\) is the number of attempts made, including the first successful attempt.

  1. Derive the probability generating function of \(X\).

    [3]

  2. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(X)\).

    [2]

  3. Find the least integer \(N\) for which \(\mathrm P(X<N)>0.98\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Successes on different trials are independent and have the same probability. The count includes the successful trial.

\[\mathrm P(X=r)=\frac{3}{10}\left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^{r-1},\quad r=1,2,3,\ldots\]

Use the sum of a geometric series:

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{3}{10}t\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{7}{10}t\right)^j=\frac{3 t}{10 \left(1 - \frac{7 t}{10}\right)}\]

The series converges for \(|t|<\frac{10}{7}\), so evaluation and differentiation at \(t=1\) are valid.

(b)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{X}'(t)=\frac{30}{\left(7 t - 10\right)^{2}}\]
\[\mathrm E(X)=G_{X}'(1)=\frac{10}{3}\]

(c)

\[\mathrm P(X<N)=1-\left(\frac7{10}\right)^{N-1}\]
\[N-1>\frac{\ln(0.02)}{\ln(0.7)}=10.968034\]

Thus \(N=12\). The preceding integer fails:

\[\mathrm P(X<11)=0.971752,\quad\mathrm P(X<12)=0.980227\]

questions.title: Failures before a successful transmission
questions.prompt_html:
A transmitter sends independent messages until one is received correctly. Each message succeeds with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). Let \(F\) count only the failed messages before the first success.

  1. State the possible values of \(F\) and derive its PGF.

    [3]

  2. Find \(\mathrm P(F=4)\) and \(\mathrm P(F\ge3)\).

    [2]

  3. Find the greatest positive integer \(n\) for which \(\mathrm P(F<n)<0.97\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Successes on different trials are independent and have the same probability. The count excludes the successful trial.

\[\mathrm P(F=r)=\frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^r,\quad r=0,1,2,\ldots\]

Use the sum of a geometric series:

\[G_{F}(t)=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{3}{5}t\right)^r=\frac{2}{5 \left(1 - \frac{3 t}{5}\right)}\]

The series converges for \(|t|<\frac{5}{3}\), so evaluation and differentiation at \(t=1\) are valid.

(b)

\[\mathrm P(F=4)=\left(\frac35\right)^4\frac25=\frac{162}{3125}\]
\[\mathrm P(F\ge3)=\left(\frac35\right)^3=\frac{27}{125}\]

(c)

\[\mathrm P(F<n)=1-(3/5)^n<0.97\iff n<\frac{\ln(0.03)}{\ln(0.6)}\]

The bound is \(6.864491\), giving \(n=6\). At \(n=7\) the probability already exceeds 0.97.

questions.title: Scheduled checks on three days each week
questions.prompt_html:
A laboratory runs an independent diagnostic check every Monday, Wednesday and Friday, beginning on a Monday. The probability that a check detects a fault is a constant \(p\). The probability that the first three checks all fail to detect the fault is 0.343. Let \(X\) be the number of checks until the first detection, including that check.

  1. Find \(p\) and derive \(G_X(t)\).

    [3]

  2. Find the probability that the first detection is on Friday of the second week.

    [2]

  3. Find the least integer \(N\) such that \(\mathrm P(X\le N)>0.96\). State the corresponding day and week.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(p=3/10,\quad G_X(t)=\frac{3 t}{10 \left(1 - \frac{7 t}{10}\right)}\)

(b)

\(\mathrm P(X=6)=\frac{50421}{1000000}\)

(c)

\(N=10\); Monday of week 4.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[(1-p)^3=0.343=(0.7)^3\Rightarrow p=0.3\]

Successes on different trials are independent and have the same probability. The count includes the successful trial.

\[\mathrm P(X=r)=\frac{3}{10}\left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^{r-1},\quad r=1,2,3,\ldots\]

Use the sum of a geometric series:

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{3}{10}t\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{7}{10}t\right)^j=\frac{3 t}{10 \left(1 - \frac{7 t}{10}\right)}\]

The series converges for \(|t|<\frac{10}{7}\), so evaluation and differentiation at \(t=1\) are valid.

(b)

The checks in week 1 are numbers 1, 2, 3; Friday in week 2 is check 6.

\[\mathrm P(X=6)=(0.7)^5(0.3)=\frac{50421}{1000000}\]

(c)

\[1-(0.7)^N>0.96\iff N>\frac{\ln0.04}{\ln0.7}\]

The bound is 9.024676. Hence \(N=10\), which is Monday of week 4.

The probability at \(N-1\) is 0.959646; at \(N\) it is 0.971752.

(b)

(c)

questions.prompt_html:
Each test of a component is successful only if two independent checks both pass. Their pass probabilities are \(2/3\) and \(3/5\). Tests are independent and identically conducted. Let \(X\) be the number of tests up to and including the first successful test.

    [2]

  3. Given that no success occurs in the first four tests, find the probability that more than nine tests are needed in total.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[p=\frac23\cdot\frac35=\frac25\]

Successes on different trials are independent and have the same probability. The count includes the successful trial.

\[\mathrm P(X=r)=\frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{r-1},\quad r=1,2,3,\ldots\]

Use the sum of a geometric series:

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{2}{5}t\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{3}{5}t\right)^j=\frac{2 t}{5 \left(1 - \frac{3 t}{5}\right)}\]

The series converges for \(|t|<\frac{5}{3}\), so evaluation and differentiation at \(t=1\) are valid.

(b)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{X}'(t)=\frac{10}{\left(3 t - 5\right)^{2}}\]
\[\mathrm E(X)=G_{X}'(1)=\frac{5}{2}\]

(c)

\[\mathrm P(X>9\mid X>4)=\frac{\mathrm P(X>9)}{\mathrm P(X>4)}=\frac{(3/5)^9}{(3/5)^4}=(3/5)^5\]

questions.title: Recovering a success probability from the variance
questions.prompt_html:
Independent inspections detect a defect with the same probability \(p\), where \(0<p<1\). Let \(X\) be the number of inspections including the first detection. It is known that \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=12\).

  1. Derive \(G_X(t)=\dfrac{pt}{1-(1-p)t}\).

    [3]

  2. Use derivatives of the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\) in terms of \(p\), and hence find \(p\).

    [4]

  3. Find \(\mathrm P(3\le X\le6)\).

    [2]

  4. Find the least integer \(N\) for which \(\mathrm P(X\le N)>0.99\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For \(r\ge1\), \(\mathrm P(X=r)=p(1-p)^{r-1}\). Therefore

\[G_X(t)=pt\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}[(1-p)t]^j=\frac{pt}{1-(1-p)t}\]

(b)

\[G'_X(1)=\frac1p,\qquad G''_X(1)=\frac{2(1-p)}{p^2}\]
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{2(1-p)}{p^2}+\frac1p-\frac1{p^2}=\frac{1-p}{p^2}\]
\[12p^2+p-1=(4p-1)(3p+1)=0\]

The roots are \(p=1/4\) and \(p=-1/3\). Only \(p=1/4\) is a probability.

(c)

\[\mathrm P(3\le X\le6)=\mathrm P(X>2)-\mathrm P(X>6)=(3/4)^2-(3/4)^6=\frac{1575}{4096}\]

(d)

\[N>\frac{\ln0.01}{\ln(3/4)}\]

Thus \(N=17\). The values at \(N-1\) and \(N\) are 0.989977 and 0.992483 respectively.

(b)

(c)

questions.title: A PGF with gaps in its support
questions.prompt_html:
The random variable \(Y\) takes values \(0,3,6,9,\ldots\) and has PGF

(a)

\[G_Y(1)=\frac{k}{1-a}=1\Rightarrow k=1-a\]

\[G_Y(t)=(1-a)\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a^jt^{3j}\]

questions.title: Signals from two independent sensor groups
questions.prompt_html:
Three independent sensors activate with probabilities \(1/2\), \(2/5\) and \(3/4\). Let \(X\) count their activations. A separate pair of independent sensors each activates with probability \(1/3\); let \(Y\) count these activations. All five sensors operate independently, and \(Z=X+Y\).

  1. Find \(G_X(t)\) as a polynomial.

    [3]

  2. Find \(G_Z(t)\) as an expanded polynomial.

    [4]

  3. Use \(G_Z\) to find \(\mathrm E(Z)\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(G_X(t)=\frac{3 t^{3}}{20} + \frac{17 t^{2}}{40} + \frac{7 t}{20} + \frac{3}{40}\)

(b)

\(G_Z(t)=\frac{t^{5}}{60} + \frac{41 t^{4}}{360} + \frac{53 t^{3}}{180} + \frac{127 t^{2}}{360} + \frac{17 t}{90} + \frac{1}{30}\)

(c)

\(\mathrm E(Z)=\frac{139}{60}\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For a single indicator with success probability \(p\), the PGF is \(1-p+pt\). Multiply these factors because the indicators are independent.

\[G_{X}(t)=\left(\frac{t}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{2 t}{5} + \frac{3}{5}\right)\left(\frac{3 t}{4} + \frac{1}{4}\right)\]
\[=\frac{3 t^{3}}{20} + \frac{17 t^{2}}{40} + \frac{7 t}{20} + \frac{3}{40}\]

(b)

\[G_Y(t)=\frac{t^{2}}{9} + \frac{4 t}{9} + \frac{4}{9}\]

Independence allows the PGFs to be multiplied:

\[G_{Z}(t)=G_{X}(t)G_{Y}(t)\]
\[=(\frac{3 t^{3}}{20} + \frac{17 t^{2}}{40} + \frac{7 t}{20} + \frac{3}{40})(\frac{t^{2}}{9} + \frac{4 t}{9} + \frac{4}{9})\]
\[=\frac{t^{5}}{60} + \frac{41 t^{4}}{360} + \frac{53 t^{3}}{180} + \frac{127 t^{2}}{360} + \frac{17 t}{90} + \frac{1}{30}\]

(c)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Z}'(t)=\frac{\left(t + 2\right) \left(15 t^{3} + 52 t^{2} + 55 t + 17\right)}{180}\]
\[\mathrm E(Z)=G_{Z}'(1)=\frac{139}{60}\]

questions.title: A normalising constant and a sparse total
questions.prompt_html:
Independent random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) have PGFs

\[G_X(t)=k(2+t+3t^2),\qquad G_Y(t)=\frac{t(3+2t^2)}5.\]

Let \(Z=X+Y\).

  1. Find \(k\) and \(\mathrm E(X)\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(G_Z(t)\) as an expanded polynomial.

    [3]

  3. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(Z)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\).

    [3]

  4. State every most probable value of \(Z\).

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(k=\frac16,\quad\mathrm E(X)=\frac76\)

(b)

\(G_Z(t)=\frac{t^{5}}{5} + \frac{t^{4}}{15} + \frac{13 t^{3}}{30} + \frac{t^{2}}{10} + \frac{t}{5}\)

(c)

\(\mathrm E(Z)=\frac{89}{30},\quad\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{1589}{900}\).

(d)

\(Z=3\) is the unique mode.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[G_X(1)=6k=1\Rightarrow k=\frac16\]
\[G'_X(t)=\frac{1+6t}{6},\quad G'_X(1)=\frac76\]

(b)

Independence allows the PGFs to be multiplied:

\[G_{Z}(t)=G_{X}(t)G_{Y}(t)\]
\[=(\frac{t^{2}}{2} + \frac{t}{6} + \frac{1}{3})(\frac{t \left(2 t^{2} + 3\right)}{5})\]
\[=\frac{t^{5}}{5} + \frac{t^{4}}{15} + \frac{13 t^{3}}{30} + \frac{t^{2}}{10} + \frac{t}{5}\]

(c)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Z}'(t)=\frac{30 t^{4} + 8 t^{3} + 39 t^{2} + 6 t + 6}{30}\]
\[\mathrm E(Z)=G_{Z}'(1)=\frac{89}{30}\]
\[G_{Z}''(t)=\frac{20 t^{3} + 4 t^{2} + 13 t + 1}{5}\]
\[G_{Z}''(1)=\frac{38}{5}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(Z^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2=\frac{1589}{900}\]

(d)

The largest coefficient is \(\frac{13}{30}\), occurring at \(t^{3}\). Therefore \(Z=3\) is the unique mode.

(a)

(b)

Use the product rule only after identifying the independent variables.

(c)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2\).

A game has three independent blue targets, each hit with probability \(3/5\), and two independent white targets, each hit with probability \(1/4\). All five outcomes are independent. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) count blue and white hits respectively. The total score is \(Z=2X+Y\).

  2. Starting from \(G_{2X}(t)=\mathrm E(t^{2X})\), find \(G_Z(t)\) as an expanded polynomial.

    [4]

    [2]

(a)

\(G_X(t)=\frac{27 t^{3}}{125} + \frac{54 t^{2}}{125} + \frac{36 t}{125} + \frac{8}{125}\)

(b)

\(G_Z(t)=\frac{27 t^{8}}{2000} + \frac{81 t^{7}}{1000} + \frac{297 t^{6}}{2000} + \frac{81 t^{5}}{500} + \frac{261 t^{4}}{1000} + \frac{27 t^{3}}{250} + \frac{83 t^{2}}{500} + \frac{3 t}{125} + \frac{9}{250}\)

\(\mathrm E(Z)=\frac{41}{10}\).

(a)

The three blue-hit indicators are independent, each with PGF \((2+3t)/5\).

\[G_X(t)=\left(\frac{3 t}{5} + \frac{2}{5}\right)^{3}=\frac{27 t^{3}}{125} + \frac{54 t^{2}}{125} + \frac{36 t}{125} + \frac{8}{125}\]

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Z}'(t)=\frac{\left(t + 3\right) \left(3 t^{2} + 2\right)^{2} \left(12 t^{2} + 27 t + 2\right)}{1000}\]
\[\mathrm E(Z)=G_{Z}'(1)=\frac{41}{10}\]

    [2]

    [1]

(a)

\(G_X(t)=\frac{t^{2}}{9} + \frac{4 t}{9} + \frac{4}{9}\)

\(G_Y(t)=\frac{16 t^{3}}{125} + \frac{52 t^{2}}{125} + \frac{48 t}{125} + \frac{9}{125}\)

\(G_Z(t)=\frac{16 t^{5}}{1125} + \frac{116 t^{4}}{1125} + \frac{64 t^{3}}{225} + \frac{409 t^{2}}{1125} + \frac{76 t}{375} + \frac{4}{125}\)

(a)

questions.title: Deriving the Poisson generating function
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(X\) have a Poisson distribution with parameter \(\lambda>0\). You may use the series \(e^z=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}z^r/r!\).

  1. Starting from the probability mass function, prove that \(G_X(t)=e^{\lambda(t-1)}\).

    [3]

  2. Use this PGF to obtain the mean and variance of \(X\).

    [3]

  3. By evaluating \(G_X(-1)\), find the probability that \(X\) is even. Include zero as even.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\mathrm P(X=r)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^r}{r!},\quad r=0,1,2,\ldots\]
\[G_X(t)=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^r t^r}{r!}=e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda t}=e^{\lambda(t-1)}\]

(b)

\[G'_X(t)=\lambda e^{\lambda(t-1)},\quad G''_X(t)=\lambda^2 e^{\lambda(t-1)}\]
\[\mathrm E(X)=\lambda,\quad\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda^2+\lambda-\lambda^2=\lambda\]

(c)

Since \((-1)^r\) is +1 for even \(r\) and −1 for odd \(r\),

\[G_X(-1)=P_{\rm even}-P_{\rm odd}=e^{-2\lambda},\qquad P_{\rm even}+P_{\rm odd}=1\]
\[P_{\rm even}=\frac{1+e^{-2\lambda}}2\]

(b)

(a)

\(G_X(t)=\frac{t^{3}}{12} + \frac{3 t^{2}}{8} + \frac{5 t}{12} + \frac{1}{8}\)

(b)

\(G_Z(t)=\frac{t^{7}}{192} + \frac{3 t^{6}}{128} + \frac{11 t^{5}}{192} + \frac{19 t^{4}}{128} + \frac{13 t^{3}}{64} + \frac{33 t^{2}}{128} + \frac{15 t}{64} + \frac{9}{128}\)

(c)

\(\mathrm E(Z)=\frac{29}{12}\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For a single indicator with success probability \(p\), the PGF is \(1-p+pt\). Multiply these factors because the indicators are independent.

\[G_{X}(t)=\left(\frac{t}{4} + \frac{3}{4}\right)\left(\frac{t}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{2 t}{3} + \frac{1}{3}\right)\]
\[=\frac{t^{3}}{12} + \frac{3 t^{2}}{8} + \frac{5 t}{12} + \frac{1}{8}\]

(b)

A successful die roll has probability \(2/8=1/4\).

\[G_Y(t)=\left(\frac{t}{4} + \frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}\]

\[G_Z(t)=G_X(t)G_Y(t^2)=\frac{t^{7}}{192} + \frac{3 t^{6}}{128} + \frac{11 t^{5}}{192} + \frac{19 t^{4}}{128} + \frac{13 t^{3}}{64} + \frac{33 t^{2}}{128} + \frac{15 t}{64} + \frac{9}{128}\]

(c)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[\mathrm E(Z)=G_{Z}'(1)=\frac{29}{12}\]

(c)

Only the terms in \(t^4\) and \(t^5\) contribute:

\[\mathrm P(Z>3)=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{2}\]

(d)

questions.title: An exact tail for a five-indicator total
questions.prompt_html:
A unit contains three independent primary sensors, each with activation probability \(2/5\), and two independent backup sensors, each with probability \(1/2\). All five are independent. \(X\) is the primary count and \(Z\) the total count.

  1. Find \(G_X(t)\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(G_Z(t)\) as a polynomial, explaining the additional factor you use.

    [3]

  3. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(Z)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\).

    [3]

  4. Use the PGF to find the probability that at least four sensors activate.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(G_X(t)=\frac{8 t^{3}}{125} + \frac{36 t^{2}}{125} + \frac{54 t}{125} + \frac{27}{125}\)

(b)

\(G_Z(t)=\frac{2 t^{5}}{125} + \frac{13 t^{4}}{125} + \frac{67 t^{3}}{250} + \frac{171 t^{2}}{500} + \frac{27 t}{125} + \frac{27}{500}\)

(c)

\(\mathrm E(Z)=\frac{11}{5},\quad\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{61}{50}\).

(d)

\(\frac{3}{25}\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For a single indicator with success probability \(p\), the PGF is \(1-p+pt\). Multiply these factors because the indicators are independent.

\[G_{X}(t)=\left(\frac{2 t}{5} + \frac{3}{5}\right)\left(\frac{2 t}{5} + \frac{3}{5}\right)\left(\frac{2 t}{5} + \frac{3}{5}\right)\]
\[=\frac{8 t^{3}}{125} + \frac{36 t^{2}}{125} + \frac{54 t}{125} + \frac{27}{125}\]

(b)

Independence allows the PGFs to be multiplied:

\[G_{Z}(t)=G_{X}(t)G_{Y}(t)\]
\[=(\frac{8 t^{3}}{125} + \frac{36 t^{2}}{125} + \frac{54 t}{125} + \frac{27}{125})(\frac{t^{2}}{4} + \frac{t}{2} + \frac{1}{4})\]
\[=\frac{2 t^{5}}{125} + \frac{13 t^{4}}{125} + \frac{67 t^{3}}{250} + \frac{171 t^{2}}{500} + \frac{27 t}{125} + \frac{27}{500}\]

(c)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Z}'(t)=\frac{\left(t + 1\right) \left(2 t + 3\right)^{2} \left(5 t + 6\right)}{250}\]
\[\mathrm E(Z)=G_{Z}'(1)=\frac{11}{5}\]
\[G_{Z}''(t)=\frac{\left(2 t + 3\right) \left(40 t^{2} + 96 t + 57\right)}{250}\]
\[G_{Z}''(1)=\frac{193}{50}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(Z^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2=\frac{61}{50}\]

(d)

\[\mathrm P(Z\ge4)=[t^4]G_Z(t)+[t^5]G_Z(t)=\frac{13}{125}+\frac{2}{125}=\frac{3}{25}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

(b)

Use the product rule only after identifying the independent variables.

(c)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2\).

(d)

At least four includes totals 4 and 5 only.

questions.title: Factorial moments and a shifted infinite total
questions.prompt_html:
Independent variables \(X\) and \(Y\) have PGFs

\[G_X(t)=\frac{t}{(2-t)^3},\qquad G_Y(t)=\frac{t^2}{(2-t)^2}.\]

Let \(Z=X+Y\).

  1. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

    [5]

  2. Find \(\mathrm P(Z>5)\) using the PGF of \(Z\).

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{X}'(t)=\frac{2 \left(t + 1\right)}{\left(t - 2\right)^{4}}\]
\[\mathrm E(X)=G_{X}'(1)=4\]
\[G_{X}''(t)=- \frac{6 \left(t + 2\right)}{\left(t - 2\right)^{5}}\]
\[G_{X}''(1)=18\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(X^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=G_{X}''(1)+G_{X}'(1)-[G_{X}'(1)]^2=6\]

(b)

\[G_Z(t)=\frac{t^3}{(2-t)^5}=\frac{t^3}{32}\left(1-\frac t2\right)^{-5}\]

The smallest possible total is 3. Only the constant, linear and quadratic terms of the remaining factor are needed:

\[\left(1-\frac t2\right)^{-5}=1+\frac52t+\frac{15}{4}t^2+\cdots\]
\[\mathrm P(Z>5)=1-\frac1{32}\left(1+\frac52+\frac{15}{4}\right)=\frac{99}{128}\]

(a)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=G_{X}''(1)+G_{X}'(1)-[G_{X}'(1)]^2\).

(b)

Find the smallest supported total before choosing the coefficients for the complement.

questions.title: A shifted polynomial PGF
questions.prompt_html:
The variable \(X\) has PGF \(G_X(t)=ct^2(2+t)^4\), where \(c\) is a constant. Let \(Y\) be the sum of three independent observations of \(X\).

\[G_X(1)=81c=1\Rightarrow c=1/81\]

\[G_Y(t)=[G_X(t)]^3=\frac{t^6(2+t)^{12}}{3^{12}}\]

questions.title: Failures, attempts and independent repetitions
questions.prompt_html:
Independent trials succeed with probability \(p\), where \(0<p<1\). The variable \(F\) counts failures before the first success; \(T=F+1\) counts all trials up to that success.

\[\mathrm P(F=r)=p(1-p)^r,\quad r=0,1,2,\ldots\]

questions.title: Different populations, independent selections
questions.prompt_html:
Box A contains 4 green and 5 orange counters. A uniform selection of three without replacement gives a green count \(X\). Independently, two counters are selected without replacement from box B, containing 3 green and 4 orange counters; the green count is \(Y\). Let \(Z=X+Y\).

  1. Find \(G_X(t)\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(G_Y(t)\) and \(G_Z(t)\) as polynomials.

    [3]

  3. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(Z)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(G_X(t)=\frac{t^{3}}{21} + \frac{5 t^{2}}{14} + \frac{10 t}{21} + \frac{5}{42}\)

(b)

\(G_Y(t)=\frac{t^{2}}{7} + \frac{4 t}{7} + \frac{2}{7}\)

\(G_Z(t)=\frac{t^{5}}{147} + \frac{23 t^{4}}{294} + \frac{2 t^{3}}{7} + \frac{115 t^{2}}{294} + \frac{10 t}{49} + \frac{5}{147}\)

(c)

\(\mathrm E(Z)=\frac{46}{21},\quad\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{425}{441}\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

There are \(\binom{9}{3}=84\) equally likely selections. To obtain \(r\) successes, choose \(r\) from the 4 marked items and \(3-r\) from the others.

\[\mathrm P(X=r)=\frac{\binom{4}{r}\binom{5}{3-r}}{\binom{9}{3}}\]
Probability distribution
\(X\)\(\mathrm P(X=x)\)
0\(\frac{5}{42}\)
1\(\frac{10}{21}\)
2\(\frac{5}{14}\)
3\(\frac{1}{21}\)
\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{t^{3}}{21} + \frac{5 t^{2}}{14} + \frac{10 t}{21} + \frac{5}{42}\]

(b)

There are \(\binom{7}{2}=21\) equally likely selections. To obtain \(r\) successes, choose \(r\) from the 3 marked items and \(2-r\) from the others.

\[\mathrm P(Y=r)=\frac{\binom{3}{r}\binom{4}{2-r}}{\binom{7}{2}}\]
Probability distribution
\(Y\)\(\mathrm P(Y=x)\)
0\(\frac{2}{7}\)
1\(\frac{4}{7}\)
2\(\frac{1}{7}\)
\[G_{Y}(t)=\frac{t^{2}}{7} + \frac{4 t}{7} + \frac{2}{7}\]

Independence allows the PGFs to be multiplied:

\[G_{Z}(t)=G_{X}(t)G_{Y}(t)\]
\[=(\frac{t^{3}}{21} + \frac{5 t^{2}}{14} + \frac{10 t}{21} + \frac{5}{42})(\frac{t^{2}}{7} + \frac{4 t}{7} + \frac{2}{7})\]
\[=\frac{t^{5}}{147} + \frac{23 t^{4}}{294} + \frac{2 t^{3}}{7} + \frac{115 t^{2}}{294} + \frac{10 t}{49} + \frac{5}{147}\]

(c)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Z}'(t)=\frac{\left(t + 1\right) \left(5 t^{3} + 41 t^{2} + 85 t + 30\right)}{147}\]
\[\mathrm E(Z)=G_{Z}'(1)=\frac{46}{21}\]
\[G_{Z}''(t)=\frac{20 t^{3} + 138 t^{2} + 252 t + 115}{147}\]
\[G_{Z}''(1)=\frac{25}{7}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(Z^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2=\frac{425}{441}\]

(a)

(b)

questions.title: Reconstructing a missing coefficient in a PGF
questions.prompt_html:
The variable \(Y\) is the sum of two independent observations of a non-negative integer-valued variable \(X\). Its PGF is

\[G_Y(t)=\frac{4+20t+25t^2+4t^3+10t^4+t^6}{64}.\]

  1. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(Y)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(G_X(t)\) as a polynomial. Explain why the sign of its constant coefficient is fixed.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Y}'(t)=\frac{\left(3 t^{2} + 5\right) \left(t^{3} + 5 t + 2\right)}{32}\]
\[\mathrm E(Y)=G_{Y}'(1)=2\]
\[G_{Y}''(t)=\frac{15 t^{4} + 60 t^{2} + 12 t + 25}{32}\]
\[G_{Y}''(1)=\frac{7}{2}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(Y^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(Y)=G_{Y}''(1)+G_{Y}'(1)-[G_{Y}'(1)]^2=\frac{3}{2}\]

(b)

The highest possible value of \(Y\) is 6, so the highest possible value of each identically distributed non-negative summand is 3. Write \(G_X(t)=a+bt+ct^2+dt^3\). Its coefficients are probabilities and cannot be negative.

\[a^2=\frac4{64}\Rightarrow a=\frac14\]
\[2ab=\frac{20}{64}\Rightarrow b=\frac58\]
\[b^2+2ac=\frac{25}{64}\Rightarrow c=0\]
\[2ad+2bc=\frac4{64}\Rightarrow d=\frac18\]
\[G_X(t)=\frac{t^{3}}{8} + \frac{5 t}{8} + \frac{1}{4}\]

Squaring this polynomial reproduces every coefficient of \(G_Y\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=G_{Y}''(1)+G_{Y}'(1)-[G_{Y}'(1)]^2\).

(b)

Use coefficients in increasing order and non-negativity.

questions.title: Two repeated binary experiments
questions.prompt_html:
A binary experiment A succeeds with probability \(2/5\) and is performed twice. Let \(X\) count successes. Independently, binary experiment B succeeds with probability \(1/2\) and is performed twice; \(Y\) counts its successes. All four trials are independent, and \(Z=X+Y\).

  1. Find \(G_X(t)\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(G_Z(t)\) as an expanded polynomial.

    [3]

  3. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(Z)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\).

    [3]

  4. State every most probable value of \(Z\).

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(G_X(t)=\frac{4 t^{2}}{25} + \frac{12 t}{25} + \frac{9}{25}\)

(b)

\(G_Z(t)=\frac{t^{4}}{25} + \frac{t^{3}}{5} + \frac{37 t^{2}}{100} + \frac{3 t}{10} + \frac{9}{100}\)

(c)

\(\mathrm E(Z)=\frac{9}{5},\quad\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{49}{50}\).

(d)

\(Z=2\) is the unique mode.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For a single indicator with success probability \(p\), the PGF is \(1-p+pt\). Multiply these factors because the indicators are independent.

\[G_{X}(t)=\left(\frac{2 t}{5} + \frac{3}{5}\right)\left(\frac{2 t}{5} + \frac{3}{5}\right)\]
\[=\frac{4 t^{2}}{25} + \frac{12 t}{25} + \frac{9}{25}\]

(b)

Independence allows the PGFs to be multiplied:

\[G_{Z}(t)=G_{X}(t)G_{Y}(t)\]
\[=(\frac{4 t^{2}}{25} + \frac{12 t}{25} + \frac{9}{25})(\frac{t^{2}}{4} + \frac{t}{2} + \frac{1}{4})\]
\[=\frac{t^{4}}{25} + \frac{t^{3}}{5} + \frac{37 t^{2}}{100} + \frac{3 t}{10} + \frac{9}{100}\]

(c)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Z}'(t)=\frac{\left(t + 1\right) \left(2 t + 3\right) \left(4 t + 5\right)}{50}\]
\[\mathrm E(Z)=G_{Z}'(1)=\frac{9}{5}\]
\[G_{Z}''(t)=\frac{24 t^{2} + 60 t + 37}{50}\]
\[G_{Z}''(1)=\frac{121}{50}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(Z^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2=\frac{49}{50}\]

(d)

The largest coefficient is \(\frac{37}{100}\), occurring at \(t^{2}\). Therefore \(Z=2\) is the unique mode.

questions.title: A sparse PGF and two identical observations
questions.prompt_html:
A discrete variable \(X\) has PGF

\[G_X(t)=\frac14t+\frac12t^3+\frac14t^4.\]

The variable \(Y\) is the sum of two independent observations of \(X\).

  1. Find \(G_Y(t)\) as an expanded polynomial. State which integer between the minimum and maximum possible totals has probability zero.

    [4]

  2. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(Y)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[G_Y(t)=[G_X(t)]^2=\frac{t^{8}}{16} + \frac{t^{7}}{4} + \frac{t^{6}}{4} + \frac{t^{5}}{8} + \frac{t^{4}}{4} + \frac{t^{2}}{16}\]

The possible totals run from 2 to 8, but there is no term in \(t^3\). There is no way to make total 3 from two values in \(\{1,3,4\}\).

(b)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Y}'(t)=\frac{t \left(t^{3} + 2 t^{2} + 1\right) \left(4 t^{3} + 6 t^{2} + 1\right)}{8}\]
\[\mathrm E(Y)=G_{Y}'(1)=\frac{11}{2}\]
\[G_{Y}''(t)=\frac{28 t^{6} + 84 t^{5} + 60 t^{4} + 20 t^{3} + 24 t^{2} + 1}{8}\]
\[G_{Y}''(1)=\frac{217}{8}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(Y^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(Y)=G_{Y}''(1)+G_{Y}'(1)-[G_{Y}'(1)]^2=\frac{19}{8}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Allow for zero coefficients rather than assuming consecutive support.

(b)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=G_{Y}''(1)+G_{Y}'(1)-[G_{Y}'(1)]^2\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the second factorial moment and use the variance identity.

questions.title: A parameterised distribution and eight copies
questions.prompt_html:
A variable \(X\) takes values 0, 1 and 3 with probabilities \(a\), \(3a\) and \(b\) respectively, where \(a,b\ge0\) and \(4a+b=1\). Let \(Y=X_1+\cdots+X_8\), where the \(X_i\) are independent observations of \(X\).

  1. Write down \(G_X(t)\) and use it to find \(\mathrm E(X)\).

    [2]

  2. Show that \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=6b+3(a+b)-9(a+b)^2\).

    [3]

  3. Use the PGF of \(Y\) to prove that \(\mathrm E(Y)=8\mathrm E(X)\).

    [3]

  4. When \(b=0\), identify the distribution of \(Y\) fully.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[G_X(t)=a+3at+bt^3,\qquad G_X^{\prime}(t)=3a+3bt^2\]
\[\mathrm E(X)=G_X^{\prime}(1)=3a+3b\]

(b)

\[G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=6bt,\quad G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=6b\]
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=6b+(3a+3b)-(3a+3b)^2\]

(c)

\[G_Y(t)=[G_X(t)]^8,\qquad G_Y^{\prime}(t)=8[G_X(t)]^7G_X^{\prime}(t)\]

Since \(G_X(1)=4a+b=1\),

\[G_Y^{\prime}(1)=8\cdot1^7G_X^{\prime}(1)=8\mathrm E(X)\]

(d)

If \(b=0\), then \(a=1/4\) and \(X\) is a binary indicator with success probability \(3/4\). Hence

\[G_Y(t)=\left(\frac14+\frac34t\right)^8\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The power is 3 for the last supported value.

(b)

Use the second factorial moment, not the raw second moment.

(c)

Use the product/chain rule and the normalisation constraint.

(d)

Find \(a\) first in the boundary case.

marking_criteria.description_html: Identify X as a Bernoulli variable with parameter 3/4.

questions.title: Five observations on an odd lattice
questions.prompt_html:
A variable \(X\) takes values 1 and 3 with probabilities \(3/5\) and \(2/5\). The variable \(Y\) is the sum of five independent observations of \(X\).

  1. Write down \(G_X(t)\).

    [1]

  2. Give \(G_Y(t)\) in factorised form and state its support.

    [2]

  3. Find \(\mathrm P(Y=9)\).

    [3]

  4. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(Y)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[G_X(t)=\frac35t+\frac25t^3\]

(b)

\[G_Y(t)=[G_X(t)]^5=\frac{t^5(3+2t^2)^5}{5^5}\]

Each change from a value 1 to a value 3 adds 2 to the total, so only these six odd totals are possible.

(c)

After removing \(t^5\), the required term has degree 4. Select \(2t^2\) from exactly two of the five factors:

\[\mathrm P(Y=9)=\frac{\binom52 3^3 2^2}{5^5}=\frac{216}{625}\]

(d)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Y}'(t)=\frac{3 t^{4} \left(2 t^{2} + 1\right) \left(2 t^{2} + 3\right)^{4}}{625}\]
\[\mathrm E(Y)=G_{Y}'(1)=9\]
\[G_{Y}''(t)=\frac{12 t^{3} \left(2 t^{2} + 3\right)^{3} \left(14 t^{4} + 15 t^{2} + 3\right)}{625}\]
\[G_{Y}''(1)=\frac{384}{5}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(Y^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(Y)=G_{Y}''(1)+G_{Y}'(1)-[G_{Y}'(1)]^2=\frac{24}{5}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the two probabilities as coefficients.

(b)

Start at the minimum total and count two-point increments.

(c)

A total of 9 is four above the minimum, so two observations must take value 3.

(d)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=G_{Y}''(1)+G_{Y}'(1)-[G_{Y}'(1)]^2\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the relevant exponent after removing the t⁵ factor.
Obtain the second factorial moment and use the variance identity.

questions.title: Uniform counts and a conditioned total
questions.prompt_html:
The variable \(X\) is discrete uniform on \(\{0,1,2,3,4\}\). Let \(X_1,X_2,X_3\) be independent observations of \(X\), and set \(S=X_1+X_2+X_3\).

  1. Find \(G_X(t)\) both as a polynomial and as a single fraction for \(t\ne1\). State its value at \(t=1\).

    [3]

  2. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

    [3]

  3. Use the PGF of \(S\) to find \(\mathrm P(S=4)\).

    [3]

  4. Given that \(S=4\), find \(\mathrm P(X_1=0\mid S=4)\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[G_X(t)=\frac15(1+t+t^2+t^3+t^4)\]

Sum the finite geometric progression:

\[G_X(t)=\frac{1-t^5}{5(1-t)},\quad t\ne1\]

The fraction has a removable singularity at 1. The defining polynomial gives \(G_X(1)=1\).

(b)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{X}'(t)=\frac{4 t^{3} + 3 t^{2} + 2 t + 1}{5}\]
\[\mathrm E(X)=G_{X}'(1)=2\]
\[G_{X}''(t)=\frac{2 \left(6 t^{2} + 3 t + 1\right)}{5}\]
\[G_{X}''(1)=4\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(X^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=G_{X}''(1)+G_{X}'(1)-[G_{X}'(1)]^2=2\]

(c)

\[G_S(t)=\frac{(1+t+t^2+t^3+t^4)^3}{125}\]

To obtain degree 4, the three exponents must be non-negative and sum to 4; none can then exceed 4. There are \(\binom{6}{2}=15\) such ordered triples. Equivalently, direct multiplication gives coefficient 15.

\[\mathrm P(S=4)=\frac{15}{125}=\frac3{25}\]

(d)

With \(X_1=0\), the other two values must sum to 4. The five ordered pairs are \((0,4),(1,3),(2,2),(3,1),(4,0)\).

\[\mathrm P(X_1=0,S=4)=\frac15\cdot\frac5{25}=\frac1{25}\]
\[\mathrm P(X_1=0\mid S=4)=\frac{1/25}{3/25}=\frac13\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the finite geometric-sum identity, without treating \(t=1\) as undefined for the PGF.

(b)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=G_{X}''(1)+G_{X}'(1)-[G_{X}'(1)]^2\).

(c)

Only the coefficient of degree 4 is needed; do not expand unnecessary higher powers.

(d)

Use the joint probability in the numerator, not the marginal \(\mathrm P(X_1=0)\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct fraction and its value at the removable singularity.

questions.title: Recovering a distribution from two moments
questions.prompt_html:
A variable \(X\) takes values 0, 1 and 3 only. Its mean is \(5/4\) and its variance is \(19/16\). Let \(Y\) be the sum of three independent observations of \(X\).

  1. Find all three probabilities and hence \(G_X(t)\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(G_Y(t)\) in factorised form and \(\mathrm E(Y)\).

    [2]

  3. Find \(\mathrm P(Y=3)\).

    [2]

  4. Use \(G_Y\) to find \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(G_X(t)=a+bt+ct^3\). Then

\[a+b+c=1,\qquad b+3c=\frac54\]

Also \(\mathrm E(X^2)=19/16+(5/4)^2=11/4\), so

\[b+9c=\frac{11}{4}\Rightarrow6c=\frac32\Rightarrow c=\frac14\]
\[b=\frac12,\quad a=\frac14,\qquad G_X(t)=\frac{1+2t+t^3}{4}\]

(b)

\[G_Y(t)=[G_X(t)]^3,\qquad G_Y^{\prime}(1)=3[G_X(1)]^2G_X^{\prime}(1)=\frac{15}{4}\]

(c)

A total of 3 arises from one value 3 and two zeros, or from three values 1.

\[\mathrm P(Y=3)=3\left(\frac14\right)^3+\left(\frac12\right)^3=\frac{11}{64}\]

(d)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Y}'(t)=\frac{3 \left(3 t^{2} + 2\right) \left(t^{3} + 2 t + 1\right)^{2}}{64}\]
\[\mathrm E(Y)=G_{Y}'(1)=\frac{15}{4}\]
\[G_{Y}''(t)=\frac{3 \left(t^{3} + 2 t + 1\right) \left(12 t^{4} + 18 t^{2} + 3 t + 4\right)}{32}\]
\[G_{Y}''(1)=\frac{111}{8}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(Y^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(Y)=G_{Y}''(1)+G_{Y}'(1)-[G_{Y}'(1)]^2=\frac{57}{16}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Convert the variance into a raw second moment, or use \(G''_X(1)\).

(b)

Use the cube of the PGF and differentiate at 1.

(c)

List the distinct ways to make the coefficient of \(t^3\).

(d)

Evaluate the first two derivatives at 1.

questions.title: A binomial count plus a Poisson count
questions.prompt_html:
A variable \(X\) has distribution \(\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\), where \(n\) and \(p\) are unknown, \(n\) is a positive integer and \(0<p<1\). Its mean is 4 and its variance is \(12/5\). Independently, \(Y\) is Poisson with mean \(3/2\). Let \(Z=X+Y\).

  1. Derive \(G_X(t)\) in terms of \(n\) and \(p\).

    [2]

  2. Using the mean and variance, determine \(n\) and \(p\).

    [3]

  3. Find the PGF of \(Z\).

    [2]

  4. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(Z)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\).

    [2]

  5. Find \(\mathrm P(Z=2)\) in exact form.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[G_X(t)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom nr p^r(1-p)^{n-r}t^r=(1-p+pt)^n\]

(b)

\[np=4,\quad np(1-p)=\frac{12}{5}\]
\[1-p=\frac35\Rightarrow p=\frac25,\quad n=\frac4{2/5}=10\]

These satisfy both the probability and integer constraints.

(c)

\[G_Y(t)=e^{\frac32(t-1)}\]
\[G_Z(t)=\left(\frac35+\frac25t\right)^{10}e^{\frac32(t-1)}\]

(d)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Z}'(t)=\frac{\left(2 t + 3\right)^{9} \left(6 t + 49\right) e^{\frac{3 t}{2}}}{19531250 e^{\frac{3}{2}}}\]
\[\mathrm E(Z)=G_{Z}'(1)=\frac{11}{2}\]
\[G_{Z}''(t)=\frac{3 \left(2 t + 3\right)^{8} \left(12 t^{2} + 196 t + 747\right) e^{\frac{3 t}{2}}}{39062500 e^{\frac{3}{2}}}\]
\[G_{Z}''(1)=\frac{573}{20}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(Z^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2=\frac{39}{10}\]

(e)

The possible pairs of counts are (0,2), (1,1) and (2,0). Their coefficient contributions give

\[\mathrm P(Z=2)=e^{-3/2}\left[\left(\frac35\right)^{10}\frac{(3/2)^2}{2}+10\frac25\left(\frac35\right)^9\frac32+\binom{10}{2}\left(\frac25\right)^2\left(\frac35\right)^8\right]\]
\[=\frac{14703201}{78125000 e^{\frac{3}{2}}}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Apply the binomial theorem to the defining PGF sum.

(b)

Divide variance by mean to remove \(n\).

(c)

The PGF product remains useful without expanding every term.

(d)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2\).

(e)

Keep only degrees 0, 1 and 2 in the two factors.

questions.title: Adding two unequal waiting times
questions.prompt_html:
Independent variables \(X\) and \(Y\) count trials up to and including a first success. Their respective success probabilities are \(1/2\) and \(2/3\). Let \(Z=X+Y\).

  1. Find \(G_Z(t)\).

    [3]

  2. Use partial fractions and power series to find \(\mathrm P(Z=r)\) for every possible integer \(r\).

    [4]

  3. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(Z)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\).

    [2]

  4. Find \(\mathrm P(Z\le4)\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[G_X(t)=\frac{t}{2-t},\quad G_Y(t)=\frac{2t}{3-t}\]
\[G_Z(t)=G_X(t)G_Y(t)=\frac{2t^2}{(2-t)(3-t)}\]

(b)

\[\frac1{(2-t)(3-t)}=\frac1{2-t}-\frac1{3-t}\]
\[G_Z(t)=2t^2\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac1{2^{j+1}}-\frac1{3^{j+1}}\right)t^j\]

For a total \(r\) use \(j=r-2\). Thus

\[\mathrm P(Z=r)=2\left(2^{-(r-1)}-3^{-(r-1)}\right),\quad r\ge2\]

Probabilities outside this support are zero.

(c)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Z}'(t)=- \frac{2 t \left(5 t - 12\right)}{\left(t - 3\right)^{2} \left(t - 2\right)^{2}}\]
\[\mathrm E(Z)=G_{Z}'(1)=\frac{7}{2}\]
\[G_{Z}''(t)=\frac{4 \left(5 t^{3} - 18 t^{2} + 36\right)}{\left(t - 3\right)^{3} \left(t - 2\right)^{3}}\]
\[G_{Z}''(1)=\frac{23}{2}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(Z^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2=\frac{11}{4}\]

(d)

\[\mathrm P(Z\le4)=\frac13+\frac5{18}+\frac{19}{108}=\frac{85}{108}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The geometric parameters are different, so this is not a square of one PGF.

(b)

Remove the external \(t^2\) before indexing the coefficient.

(c)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2\).

(d)

The minimum total is 2.

questions.title: Poisson parameters and the composition of a total
questions.prompt_html:
Independent Poisson variables \(X\) and \(Y\) have unknown positive means \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\). It is known that \(\mathrm E(X+Y)=5\) and \(\mathrm P(X=0)=[\mathrm P(Y=0)]^4\). Define \(Z=X+Y\).

  1. Find \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(G_Z(t)\) and identify the distribution of \(Z\).

    [2]

  3. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm P(Z=3)\).

    [2]

  4. Given that \(Z=3\), find the probability that \(X=2\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\lambda+\mu=5,\qquad e^{-\lambda}=e^{-4\mu}\Rightarrow\lambda=4\mu\]
\[5\mu=5\Rightarrow\mu=1,\quad\lambda=4\]

(b)

\[G_Z(t)=e^{4(t-1)}e^{t-1}=e^{5(t-1)}\]

This is the PGF of a Poisson distribution with parameter 5.

(c)

\[G_Z(t)=e^{-5}\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{5^rt^r}{r!}\Rightarrow\mathrm P(Z=3)=\frac{125}{6}e^{-5}\]

(d)

The joint event is exactly \(X=2,Y=1\). Independence gives

\[\mathrm P(X=2,Y=1)=\left(e^{-4}\frac{4^2}{2!}\right)\left(e^{-1}\frac{1^1}{1!}\right)=8e^{-5}\]
\[\mathrm P(X=2\mid Z=3)=\frac{8e^{-5}}{(125/6)e^{-5}}=\frac{48}{125}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the zero-count probabilities of Poisson distributions.

(b)

Multiply the PGFs rather than assuming a distribution for a sum without justification.

(c)

Extract the coefficient of \(t^3\).

(d)

Use the joint event compatible with the conditioned total.

questions.title: A randomly selected operating mode
questions.prompt_html:
Before a run, a device selects mode A with probability \(1/3\) and mode B with probability \(2/3\). Exactly one mode is used. In mode A the output \(X\) is a count from two independent trials, each with success probability \(1/2\). In mode B, \(X\) is the number of trials up to and including a first success, with independent success probability \(1/2\).

  1. Find the PGF of \(X\).

    [3]

  2. Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

    [4]

  3. Find \(\mathrm P(X\le2)\).

    [2]

  4. Explain why the product of the two conditional PGFs would be incorrect here.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(G_X(t)=\frac{(1+t)^2}{12}+\frac{2t}{3(2-t)}\)

(b)

\(\mathrm E(X)=\frac{5}{3},\quad\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{31}{18}\).

(c)

\(5/6\)

(d)

Only one mode is used; a product would describe the sum of two independently generated outputs.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Condition on the mode. The two conditional PGFs are \((1+t)^2/4\) and \(t/(2-t)\). Therefore

\[G_X(t)=\frac13\frac{(1+t)^2}{4}+\frac23\frac{t}{2-t}\]

(b)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{X}'(t)=\frac{t^{3} - 3 t^{2} + 12}{6 \left(t - 2\right)^{2}}\]
\[\mathrm E(X)=G_{X}'(1)=\frac{5}{3}\]
\[G_{X}''(t)=\frac{t^{3} - 6 t^{2} + 12 t - 24}{6 \left(t - 2\right)^{3}}\]
\[G_{X}''(1)=\frac{17}{6}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(X^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=G_{X}''(1)+G_{X}'(1)-[G_{X}'(1)]^2=\frac{31}{18}\]

(c)

\[\mathrm P(X\le2)=\frac13\cdot1+\frac23\left(1-\frac14\right)=\frac56\]

(d)

Multiplying the conditional PGFs describes a different experiment: generating a mode-A output and a mode-B output independently and adding them. Here the alternatives are mutually exclusive, so probabilities are combined by a weighted sum, not by an independent-sum product.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Weight the conditional coefficients by the mode probabilities.

(b)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=G_{X}''(1)+G_{X}'(1)-[G_{X}'(1)]^2\).

(c)

The whole support in mode A already lies below 3.

(d)

Decide whether the experiment chooses one output or adds two outputs.

questions.title: A uniform spinner and a two-spin total
questions.prompt_html:
A spinner returns each integer 1 to 5 with equal probability. Let \(X\) be one result and \(S\) the sum of two independent results.

  1. Find \(G_X(t)\).

    [2]

(b)

\(\mathrm P(A=3)=0,\qquad\mathrm P(B=3)=\frac4{25}\)

(c)

\(\mathrm E(A)=\frac{16}{5},\quad\operatorname{Var}(A)=\frac{144}{25}\).

\(\mathrm E(B)=\frac{16}{5},\quad\operatorname{Var}(B)=\frac{72}{25}\).

(a)

\[G_A(t)=\mathrm E[(t^2)^X]=G_X(t^2)=\frac{2 t^{6}}{5} + \frac{2 t^{2}}{5} + \frac{1}{5}\]

(b)

Every value of \(A\) is even. For \(B=3\), the possible ordered pairs are (0,3) and (3,0). Hence

\[\mathrm P(A=3)=0,\quad\mathrm P(B=3)=2\cdot\frac15\cdot\frac25=\frac4{25}\]

(c)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{A}'(t)=\frac{4 t \left(3 t^{4} + 1\right)}{5}\]
\[\mathrm E(A)=G_{A}'(1)=\frac{16}{5}\]
\[G_{A}''(t)=\frac{4 \left(15 t^{4} + 1\right)}{5}\]
\[G_{A}''(1)=\frac{64}{5}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(A^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(A)=G_{A}''(1)+G_{A}'(1)-[G_{A}'(1)]^2=\frac{144}{25}\]

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{B}'(t)=\frac{4 \left(3 t^{2} + 1\right) \left(2 t^{3} + 2 t + 1\right)}{25}\]
\[\mathrm E(B)=G_{B}'(1)=\frac{16}{5}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(B^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(B)=G_{B}''(1)+G_{B}'(1)-[G_{B}'(1)]^2=\frac{72}{25}\]

The variables \(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4\) are independent and each is discrete uniform on \(\{0,1,2\}\). Let \(S=X_1+X_2+X_3+X_4\).

  1. Use the PGF of \(S\) to find \(\mathrm P(S=4)\).

  2. Given that \(S=4\), find the probability that all four observations are equal.

  3. A student claims that \(S\) has the same distribution as \(4X_1\) because their means are equal. Refute the claim using PGFs.

(a)

\[G_S(t)=\frac{(1+t+t^2)^4}{81}\]

\[1\cdot1+2\cdot2+3\cdot3+2\cdot2+1\cdot1=19\]
\[\mathrm P(S=4)=\frac{19}{81}\]

(b)

Four equal observations with total 4 must all equal 1. This particular outcome has probability \((1/3)^4=1/81\). Therefore

\[\mathrm P(X_1=X_2=X_3=X_4\mid S=4)=\frac{1/81}{19/81}=\frac1{19}\]

(c)

\[G_{4X_1}(t)=\mathrm E[(t^4)^{X_1}]=G_{X_1}(t^4)=\frac{1+t^4+t^8}{3}\]

Its probability of a total 4 is \(1/3\), whereas \(\mathrm P(S=4)=19/81\). Equal means do not determine an entire distribution.
